ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The pericardium is a double‑layered sac that surrounds the heart, anchoring it and preventing over‑distension. Its layers, relations, and fluid dynamics are key to diagnosing and managing pericardial disease.

sections.p: The pericardium protects the heart, limits its movement, and provides a lubricated space for cardiac motion.
It lies within the mediastinum, posterior to the sternum and anterior to the great vessels. The serous pericardium has a visceral layer (epicardium) and a parietal layer.
b: Fibrous pericardium attaches to sternum, aorta, pulmonary trunk

sections.p: Posteriorly it is adjacent to the esophagus; anteriorly to the sternum; it encloses the roots of the great vessels.
b: Ties to phrenic nerve, vagus, sympathetic chain

sections.p: The pericardium receives arterial blood from the pericardiacophrenic, middle cardiac, and posterior intercostal arteries.
Innervation is mainly sympathetic and parasympathetic via the phrenic nerve and vagus.
b: Pain fibers travel with phrenic nerve

sections.p: It limits cardiac expansion, provides a lubricated environment, and serves as a barrier against infection.
Pericardial disease presents with chest pain, dyspnea, or muffled heart sounds. Causes include infection, autoimmune disease, malignancy, trauma, and post‑cardiac surgery.
b: Constrictive pericarditis: rigid shell, Kussmaul sign

t.b: Detects pericardial effusion, thickness, and diastolic collapse – confirms tamponade
Shows enlarged cardiac silhouette in effusion; calcification suggests constriction
Diffuse ST elevation and PR depression in acute pericarditis; electrical alternans in large effusion

sections.p: Remember that pericardial friction rub is heard best at the left lower sternal border. In tamponade, pulsus paradoxus is a key sign.
b: Constrictive pericarditis responds poorly to diuretics

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, relieve pressure, and monitor hemodynamics.
Pericarditis can mimic pleurisy, myocardial infarction, and pulmonary embolism.
b: Pulmonary embolism can cause right heart strain

sections.p: Small effusions may be missed on chest X‑ray; ECG changes can be subtle in early pericarditis.
b: Mild effusion may appear normal on echo if suboptimal view

sections.p: Use imaging and laboratory tests to confirm diagnosis and guide treatment.
